name: Fabry Disease
description: Fabry disease is a rare, inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A (α-Gal A). This deficiency leads to the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in various cells throughout the body, leading to a wide range of symptoms affecting multiple organ systems. The disease is X-linked, affecting both males and females, though females often have milder symptoms.
prognosis: Variable, depending on the severity of organ involvement and the effectiveness of treatment. Without treatment, organ damage can progress, leading to significant morbidity and reduced life expectancy.
lifeExpectancy: Reduced by approximately 10-20 years without treatment. With enzyme replacement therapy or chaperone therapy, life expectancy can be significantly improved.
diagnosticMethods: Enzyme assay (alpha-galactosidase A activity in leukocytes or plasma)
Skin biopsy (to identify Gb3 deposits in endothelial cells)

treatmentOptions.name: Renal dialysis or kidney transplant (for end-stage renal disease)
Elfabrio (pegunigalsidase alfa)
treatmentOptions.note: EMA (type II variation II/0007 adopted 5 Mar 2026). EU product information now permits infusion once every two or four weeks, halving infusion burden for eligible patients.

eli5Summary: Imagine your body has tiny workers that clean up a certain type of sugar. In Fabry disease, these workers are broken, so the sugar builds up and causes problems in your heart, kidneys, and other parts of your body. Doctors can give you medicine to help clean up the sugar or fix the broken workers.
clinicalSummary: Fabry disease (FD) is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder resulting from a deficiency in the enzyme α-galactosidase A (α-Gal A), encoded by the GLA gene. This enzymatic deficiency leads to the progressive accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and related glycosphingolipids within lysosomes of various cell types, including endothelial, epithelial, neuronal, and cardiac cells. The clinical manifestations are highly variable, ranging from mild to severe, and can include angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, corneal and lenticular opacities, renal failure, cardiomyopathy, cerebrovascular events, and gastrointestinal disturbances. Diagnosis involves enzyme assays and genetic testing. Treatment options include enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with recombinant α-Gal A and chaperone therapy with migalastat, a pharmacological chaperone that enhances the stability of certain mutant forms of α-Gal A. Supportive care addresses specific organ involvement and pain management. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent or delay the progression of organ damage and improve patient outcomes.
historicalBackground: Fabry disease was first described independently by Johannes Fabry and William Anderson in 1898. Fabry described a 13-year-old boy with angiokeratomas, while Anderson described a 39-year-old man with similar skin lesions and kidney disease. The underlying enzyme deficiency was not identified until the late 1960s, leading to the development of enzyme replacement therapy in the early 2000s.

recentBreakthroughs.title: Venglustat phase 3 PERIDOT misses primary endpoint
recentBreakthroughs.description: Sanofi reported on 2 February 2026 that venglustat failed to beat placebo on the patient-reported primary endpoint of neuropathic and abdominal pain in PERIDOT (122 patients aged ≥16); pain fell in both arms. The second phase 3, CARAT, continues.

recentBreakthroughs.title: PTC acquires BLA-stage Fabry gene therapy
recentBreakthroughs.description: On 12 August 2026 PTC Therapeutics won the auction for ST-920 out of Sangamo's bankruptcy; the rolling BLA (started December 2025) is expected to complete in Q4 2026 under accelerated approval.

recentBreakthroughs.title: Migalastat ASPIRE adolescent phase 3b results published
recentBreakthroughs.description: Molecular Genetics and Metabolism (April 2025) reported ASPIRE, a 12-month open-label phase 3b plus extension in 21 adolescents with amenable GLA variants: renal and cardiac measures and plasma lyso-Gb3 remained stable over up to 48 months with no new safety findings.

recentBreakthroughs.title: ST-920 gene therapy delivers positive eGFR slope
recentBreakthroughs.description: Registrational STAAR data reported in June 2025 showed isaralgagene civaparvovec produced a mean annualised eGFR slope of +1.965 mL/min/1.73 m²/yr at 52 weeks across all 32 dosed patients, versus negative slopes seen with marketed Fabry therapies.

recentBreakthroughs.title: Gene Therapy Shows Promise in Early Clinical Trials
recentBreakthroughs.description: Early clinical trials of gene therapy for Fabry disease have shown promising results, with sustained increases in α-Gal A activity and reductions in Gb3 accumulation in some patients. Further studies are underway to evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of this approach.

recentBreakthroughs.title: FDA Approves Migalastat for Fabry Disease
recentBreakthroughs.description: The FDA approved migalastat, an oral pharmacological chaperone, for the treatment of Fabry disease in adults with amenable GLA variants. This provides an alternative to enzyme replacement therapy for a subset of patients.
